title: Rosacea and Alcohol: Why Drinking Triggers Flares (Red Wine Worst)
excerpt: Why alcohol triggers rosacea flares, why red wine is the most common culprit, which drinks are gentler, how long a flare lasts, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Why alcohol triggers rosacea flares, why red wine is often worst, which drinks are gentler, how long flushing lasts, and when to see a dermatologist.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** alcohol does not cause rosacea, but for many people who already have it, drinking is one of the most reliable ways to set off a flare. Alcohol widens the small blood vessels in your face, and rosacea skin overreacts to exactly that kind of signal. Red wine is the drink people with rosacea most often name as their worst trigger, but any type of alcohol can do it, and the amount you drink matters more than the label on the bottle. This guide explains why it happens, which drinks tend to be worse, how long a flare lasts, and practical ways to drink less painfully if you choose to drink at all.

**The quick rules:** If drinking makes your face burn and redden for hours, or the redness stays longer each time, alcohol is probably one of your triggers. Keep a simple log for a few weeks to confirm it. Smaller amounts, slower pacing, cold drinks, and avoiding the drinks you personally react to help most people. If your redness is spreading, your eyes are sore or gritty, or bumps and thickened skin are appearing, see a doctor or dermatologist, because rosacea is very treatable and tends to get worse without treatment.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article explains general research and is not medical advice. **Book an appointment with a doctor or dermatologist if** facial redness lasts days rather than hours, you have pimple-like bumps that don't respond to acne products, your nose or cheeks are thickening or becoming bumpy, your eyes feel dry, gritty, burning, or look bloodshot often, or redness is affecting your confidence or daily life. **Get urgent care right away if** flushing after a drink comes with hives, swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, wheezing, trouble breathing, or feeling faint. That pattern points to an allergic-type reaction, not rosacea. Also get prompt care for sudden painful eye redness or changes in your vision.

## What Rosacea Is (and Why Your Face Reacts to Alcohol)

Rosacea is a long-term inflammatory skin condition that mainly affects the central face: cheeks, nose, chin, and forehead. It is common, especially in adults over 30 and in people with fair skin, though it occurs in all skin tones and is often missed in darker skin because the redness is harder to see.

It shows up in a few different ways, and many people have more than one:

- **Flushing and persistent redness.** The face reddens easily and some redness stays all the time.
- **Visible blood vessels.** Thin red lines (often called spider veins or telangiectasia) on the cheeks and nose.
- **Bumps and pimples.** Red bumps and pus-filled spots that look like acne but without blackheads.
- **Skin thickening.** Most often on the nose (rhinophyma), and much more common in men.
- **Eye symptoms (ocular rosacea).** Dry, gritty, burning, or bloodshot eyes and irritated eyelids.

Nobody fully understands what causes rosacea. Researchers point to a mix of factors: an overactive immune response in the skin, blood vessels that dilate too easily, nerves in the skin that are extra sensitive to heat and other triggers, tiny skin mites called *Demodex* that are found in higher numbers on rosacea skin, and genetics. What is clear is that rosacea skin reacts strongly to triggers that make the face flush. That's where alcohol comes in.

### How alcohol sets off a flare

Alcohol affects rosacea skin through several routes at once:

1. **It widens blood vessels.** Alcohol is a vasodilator, which means it relaxes the walls of blood vessels so more blood flows near the skin's surface. That's why many people look flushed after a drink. In rosacea, the facial blood vessels are already prone to dilating and can be slow to settle back down, so the redness is stronger and lasts longer.
2. **It produces acetaldehyde.** Your body breaks alcohol down into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound that also causes flushing. Some people clear it slowly, which is the main reason behind the classic "Asian flush." Slow clearing can stack on top of rosacea and make a flare worse.
3. **It drives inflammation.** Alcohol and acetaldehyde both promote inflammation and oxidative stress, the same processes that keep rosacea going.
4. **Some drinks carry extra triggers.** Red wine in particular contains histamine and other compounds that can widen blood vessels on their own. Drinks that are hot (mulled wine, a hot toddy) or paired with spicy food add a second and third trigger at the same time.
5. **It can disrupt sleep and dehydrate you.** Poor sleep and stress are themselves common rosacea triggers, so a big night can lead to a rougher skin day afterwards.

The result is that one glass might give someone without rosacea a light pink glow that fades quickly, while the same glass can give someone with rosacea a burning, blotchy flare that lasts for hours.

## Does Alcohol Cause Rosacea?

This is one of the most common questions, and the answer is no, not directly. Plenty of people who never drink have rosacea, and most people who drink never get it. Alcohol is best described as a **trigger** for people who are already prone to the condition.

That said, there is evidence that drinking is linked to a higher chance of developing rosacea over time. A large study of women in the US Nurses' Health Study II, published in the *Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology* in 2017, followed tens of thousands of women for years. It found that women who drank more alcohol were more likely to be diagnosed with rosacea later, and the risk rose with the amount they drank. Interestingly, in that study the links were clearest for **white wine and liquor**, not red wine.

This is an observational study, so it shows an association, not proof that alcohol causes the condition. People who drink more may differ in other ways, such as sun exposure or smoking. But it fits with what doctors see: alcohol and rosacea tend to travel together, and heavier drinking makes things worse.

### The "drinker's nose" myth

For a long time, a red, bulbous nose (rhinophyma) was blamed on heavy drinking, partly thanks to famous comedians and cartoon drunks. This is a myth. Rhinophyma is a form of rosacea, and people who don't drink at all can develop it. Alcohol can make the redness of rosacea worse, but a bumpy, enlarged nose is not a sign that someone drinks heavily. The stigma is unfair and keeps some people from seeking treatment, which is a shame, because rhinophyma can be treated with medication early on and with procedures later.

## Why Red Wine Is the Worst for Rosacea

Ask people with rosacea which drink bothers them most and red wine comes up again and again. In patient surveys run by the National Rosacea Society, red wine has been the alcoholic drink most frequently reported as a trigger, ahead of white wine, beer, and spirits. There are several likely reasons:

- **Histamine.** Red wine generally contains more histamine than white wine, beer, or clear spirits. Histamine widens blood vessels and causes flushing. Some people break histamine down slowly, which makes this worse. Our guide to [histamine intolerance and alcohol](/never-hungover/histamine-intolerance-and-alcohol) explains this in more detail.
- **Other compounds from the grape skins.** Red wine is fermented with the skins, so it carries more tannins, phenolic compounds, and other substances that can affect blood vessels and set off headaches and flushing in sensitive people.
- **Habit and setting.** Red wine is often drunk with rich, spicy, or warm food, and often in warm restaurants. Each of those is its own trigger, so a red wine dinner can stack several triggers at once.

It's worth being clear about what the evidence does and doesn't say. Red wine being the most commonly *reported* trigger is not the same as red wine being the only problem. The large women's study mentioned above found white wine and liquor more strongly linked to developing rosacea in the first place. And many people react to all alcohol. The most useful approach is to find out how **your** skin responds rather than relying on a general ranking.

Sulfites in wine get blamed for a lot of reactions, but they are found in both red and white wine (white wine often has more), and there's no good evidence that sulfites are a major rosacea trigger for most people. If you're curious about them, see our article on [sulfites in wine and headaches](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches).

## What's the Best Alcohol for Rosacea?

There is no drink that is guaranteed to be safe for rosacea. Ethanol itself widens blood vessels, so any alcoholic drink can cause a flare if you drink enough of it. But some choices are gentler for many people. Here's a general guide, not a promise:

| Drink | General pattern for rosacea | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Red wine | Most often reported as a trigger | Higher histamine and grape-skin compounds; often paired with warm, rich food |
| White wine and champagne | Commonly reported, usually less than red | Still contains histamine and alcohol; linked to rosacea risk in one large study |
| Beer | Varies widely | Moderate alcohol per glass, but large servings add up; some people react to ingredients |
| Clear spirits (vodka, gin, tequila) | Often tolerated better in small amounts | Fewer extra compounds, but strong alcohol content; mixers matter |
| Dark spirits (whiskey, rum, brandy) | Mixed | More compounds from barrel aging than clear spirits |
| Hot or spicy drinks (mulled wine, hot toddy, spicy margarita) | Often worst | Heat and spice are separate rosacea triggers on top of the alcohol |

A few practical takeaways:

- **Many people with rosacea find a small amount of a clear spirit with a cold, non-spicy mixer easier to tolerate than red wine.** That's personal experience reported by many patients, not a guarantee.
- **The dose matters more than the drink.** Two drinks of anything will usually cause more redness than one.
- **Cold is your friend.** A cold drink served with ice is less likely to warm your face than a warm one.
- **Watch the mixers.** Spicy rims, chili-infused drinks, and hot cocktails add separate triggers.

## How Long Does a Rosacea Flare From Alcohol Last?

It varies from person to person and from night to night. Common patterns include:

- **Immediate flushing.** Redness and warmth often start within minutes of the first drink and can build as you keep drinking.
- **Hours of redness.** For many people the redness fades over several hours after they stop drinking, often by the next morning.
- **Next-day aftermath.** Some people wake up with lingering redness, swelling, or new bumps that take a few days to calm down, especially after a heavy night.
- **Gradual worsening over time.** Repeated flushing may contribute to more persistent redness and visible blood vessels over months and years. This is one reason dermatologists encourage people to manage their triggers rather than ignore them.

If redness from a single night of drinking routinely lasts more than a couple of days, or the background redness is getting worse over time, that's a good reason to see a doctor about treatment.

## Rosacea Flare or Alcohol Flush? How to Tell the Difference

Not every red face after a drink is rosacea. A few other conditions look similar, and the advice is different for each.

**Rosacea flare:**
- Redness centered on the cheeks, nose, chin, and forehead
- Often burning or stinging
- Also triggered by sun, heat, spicy food, stress, exercise, or hot drinks, not just alcohol
- May come with bumps, visible blood vessels, or eye irritation
- Some redness may be present even when you haven't been drinking

**Alcohol flush reaction (often called Asian flush):**
- Redness that can spread to the neck, chest, and body
- Often comes with a fast heartbeat, headache, or nausea after a small amount of alcohol
- Caused by slow clearing of acetaldehyde due to a common genetic variant in an enzyme called ALDH2
- Happens with alcohol specifically, not with sun or spicy food

**Allergic or histamine-type reaction:**
- Hives, itching, or a stuffy or runny nose
- May happen with specific drinks (often wine or beer)
- **Swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, wheezing, or trouble breathing is an emergency.** Call 911 or your local emergency number.

You can have more than one of these at once. If you want to dig into the general causes of facial redness after drinking, see our guide to [why your face turns red after drinking](/never-hungover/red-face-after-drinking). If puffiness rather than redness is your main issue, our article on [alcohol face bloating](/never-hungover/alcohol-face-bloating) covers that. Rosacea bumps are often mistaken for breakouts; our page on whether [alcohol causes acne](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-cause-acne) explains the difference, and if itching is your main symptom see [itchy skin after drinking](/never-hungover/itchy-skin-after-drinking).

## How to Drink With Rosacea and Have Fewer Flares

If you choose to drink, these steps help many people keep flares under control. None of them makes alcohol completely safe for rosacea skin, but together they can make a real difference.

### 1. Confirm alcohol is actually your trigger

Rosacea triggers are personal. Keep a short log for two to four weeks: what you drank, how much, what you ate, the temperature and setting, and how your skin looked that night and the next day. Many people find that alcohol is a trigger only above a certain amount, or only with certain drinks. Free rosacea diaries are available from patient organizations, or a notes app works fine.

### 2. Drink less, and drink slower

The single most effective change is drinking smaller amounts. Spacing drinks out also gives your body more time to clear alcohol and acetaldehyde, which can keep flushing milder. Alternating each alcoholic drink with a glass of cold water helps on both counts.

### 3. Pick your drinks carefully

If red wine is a problem, try switching to a small serving of something you tolerate better. Some people do fine with a single glass of white wine or a clear spirit with soda water. Others find low-alcohol or alcohol-free versions of their favorite drinks let them join in without the flush.

### 4. Keep it cold and keep the spice down

Choose cold drinks over hot ones and skip spicy food when you're drinking. Sit away from heaters, fireplaces, and hot crowded spaces when you can. Holding a cold glass to your cheek or splashing cool water on your face can calm a flush that's starting.

### 5. Don't stack triggers

Sun, heat, exercise, stress, spicy food, and hot drinks are all common rosacea triggers. A sunny afternoon drinking outside, or a hot curry with red wine, piles several on at once. If you know you'll be drinking, try to keep the other triggers low.

### 6. Look after your skin the next day

Use a gentle cleanser and moisturizer, avoid scrubbing or harsh products, and wear a broad-spectrum sunscreen (mineral sunscreens with zinc oxide are often better tolerated by rosacea skin). Drink water and get some sleep. If you use prescription rosacea treatment, keep using it as directed.

### 7. Ask about treatments that reduce redness

If you're managing rosacea on your own, it's worth knowing there are good options. A doctor or dermatologist may suggest:

- **Prescription creams for temporary redness.** Gels and creams containing brimonidine or oxymetazoline narrow facial blood vessels for several hours. Some people use them before an event. Ask your doctor whether this fits your situation, because redness can return when they wear off.
- **Treatments for bumps and inflammation.** Topical options such as metronidazole, azelaic acid, and ivermectin, and sometimes low-dose oral antibiotics such as doxycycline, which are used for their anti-inflammatory effect.
- **Procedures for blood vessels and persistent redness.** Laser and light treatments can reduce visible blood vessels and background redness.

If you take an oral antibiotic or other prescription medicine for rosacea, ask your doctor or pharmacist whether it's okay to drink with it.

## Should You Quit Drinking If You Have Rosacea?

That's your call. Some people find their rosacea is much calmer once they cut alcohol out, and decide the trade-off is worth it. Others find that one or two well-chosen drinks on occasion is fine for their skin. Many land somewhere in between: no red wine, smaller amounts, and fewer drinking nights.

A useful experiment is to take a break from alcohol for a few weeks while keeping your skincare and other habits the same, and see how your skin responds. If the difference is large, you've learned something important about your triggers. If it barely changes, alcohol may not be your main trigger and you can focus your effort elsewhere.

Whatever you decide, there's no need to feel embarrassed about flushing. Rosacea is a medical condition, not a reflection of how much someone drinks.

## Ocular Rosacea and Alcohol

Rosacea can affect the eyes, sometimes before any skin symptoms appear. Symptoms include dryness, burning, a gritty or sandy feeling, watery eyes, red eyelid margins, and recurrent styes. Alcohol can make eyes feel drier and more irritated the next day, which may aggravate ocular rosacea.

If you have ongoing eye symptoms, see a doctor or eye specialist. Ocular rosacea is treatable, and untreated it can occasionally affect the surface of the eye. **Sudden eye pain, light sensitivity, or blurry vision needs prompt medical attention.**

## Supplements and Rosacea: An Honest Word

You'll see a lot of supplements marketed for redness and flushing. The honest picture is that there's no good evidence that any supplement prevents rosacea flares from alcohol, and you should be wary of products that suggest otherwise.

Some people who drink also try **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound studied mainly for its effects on alcohol metabolism and hangovers. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents rosacea flushing, and it shouldn't replace avoiding your triggers or proper rosacea treatment. If you're interested in it for hangovers more generally, a widely available option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically use it, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicine for rosacea or anything else, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding a supplement.

For wine-specific next-day symptoms, our [wine hangover guide](/never-hungover/wine-hangover-guide) has more on why wine can hit harder than other drinks, and our guide to [preventing a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol doesn't cause rosacea, but it's one of the most common flare triggers and heavier drinking is linked to a higher chance of developing it.
- Red wine is the drink people with rosacea most often blame, likely because of histamine, grape-skin compounds, and the warm, spicy settings it's often drunk in. But any alcohol can trigger a flare.
- Amount matters more than type. Smaller, slower, colder drinks without spicy food cause fewer problems for most people.
- Keep a trigger log to find out what your skin actually reacts to.
- Rosacea is treatable. See a doctor or dermatologist if redness is persistent, bumps or thickening are appearing, or your eyes are affected. Get emergency care for swelling, hives, or trouble breathing after a drink.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does alcohol cause rosacea?**

No, alcohol doesn't directly cause rosacea, and many people with rosacea don't drink. It's a common trigger for flare-ups in people who already have the condition. A large study of US women did find that higher alcohol intake was linked to a greater chance of later being diagnosed with rosacea, but that study shows an association, not proof of cause.

**Why does red wine make my rosacea worse?**

Red wine generally contains more histamine and more compounds from grape skins than other drinks, and both can widen blood vessels and cause flushing. It's also often drunk with warm, rich, or spicy food in warm rooms, which adds more triggers. In patient surveys, red wine is the alcoholic drink most often reported as a rosacea trigger.

**What is the best alcohol to drink if you have rosacea?**

No alcohol is guaranteed to be safe for rosacea, because alcohol itself widens blood vessels. Many people find a small serving of a clear spirit, such as vodka or gin, with a cold non-spicy mixer easier to tolerate than red wine. Drinking less, drinking slowly, and keeping drinks cold usually matters more than the type.

**How long does a rosacea flare from alcohol last?**

Flushing often starts within minutes and fades over several hours after you stop drinking, often by the next morning. After a heavy night, some people have lingering redness, swelling, or new bumps for a few days. If redness from drinking routinely lasts several days or your background redness keeps getting worse, see a doctor.

**Is a red nose a sign of heavy drinking?**

No. A red, enlarged, bumpy nose (rhinophyma) is a form of rosacea, and people who never drink can develop it. Alcohol can make rosacea redness worse, but the old idea of the "drinker's nose" is a myth. Rhinophyma is treatable, especially when caught early.

**How can I tell if it's rosacea or alcohol flush?**

Rosacea redness centers on the cheeks, nose, chin, and forehead and is also triggered by sun, heat, spicy food, and stress. Alcohol flush reaction tends to spread to the neck and chest, often comes with a fast heartbeat or headache after a small amount of alcohol, and is caused by slow breakdown of acetaldehyde. If you get hives, swelling, or trouble breathing after drinking, that's an allergic-type reaction and needs emergency care.

**Can you drink alcohol while on rosacea medication?**

It depends on the medicine. Many topical rosacea creams don't have a direct interaction with alcohol, but drinking can still trigger flares that work against the treatment. If you take an oral antibiotic or another prescription medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist whether drinking is okay with it.

**Will quitting alcohol cure my rosacea?**

No. Rosacea is a long-term condition with several causes, and stopping alcohol won't make it go away. But for people whose skin reacts to alcohol, cutting back or stopping can mean fewer and milder flares. Taking a few weeks off drinking is a simple way to see how much alcohol affects your skin.
